Have you ever called customer support?

You call the helpline. The first agent picks up they can solve basic issues. If your issue is too complex, they escalate it to a senior agent. If the senior agent cannot handle it either, it goes to a specialist team.
Each person in the chain tries to handle your request. If they can't they pass it along. You never know who will ultimately solve your problem, and you don't need to.
This is exactly what the Chain of Responsibility Pattern does.
Without the pattern:
The sender has to know every possible handler. Add a new handler and you crack open this method again. Remove one and you risk breaking the whole chain.
With Chain of Responsibility:
The sender only knows the first handler. Each handler knows the next one. The request flows down the chain until someone handles it.
It is useful when:
["Multiple handlers could potentially process a request.","You want to add, remove, or reorder handlers without touching the client.","You want each handler focused on one responsibility only."]
items: Multiple handlers could potentially process a request.
You want to add, remove, or reorder handlers without touching the client.
You want each handler focused on one responsibility only.

blocks.content: Let's walk through a real example and see how it works.
1. The Problem: Processing Loan Applications
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1778245813739-1de7ab62.png
Let's say you are building a loan approval system for a bank. Every loan application must pass through several checks before it gets approved.
Before a loan gets approved, it must pass through these checks:

["Credit Score Check Is the applicant's credit score above the minimum threshold?","Income Check Does the applicant earn enough to repay the loan?","Debt Check Does the applicant have existing unpaid debt?","Loan Amount Check Is the requested amount within the approved limit?"]
items: Credit Score Check Is the applicant's credit score above the minimum threshold?
Income Check Does the applicant earn enough to repay the loan?
Debt Check Does the applicant have existing unpaid debt?
Loan Amount Check Is the requested amount within the approved limit?

blocks.content: The Naive Approach
Why This Breaks Down
1. Violates Open/Closed Principle Every new check employment verification, age check, collateral check means opening LoanProcessor and adding more if blocks. The class is never stable.

2. Poor Separation of Concerns Credit scoring logic, income logic, debt logic, and amount logic are all crammed into one method. Each check has nothing to do with the others yet they all live together. Testing one means dealing with all.
3. No Reusability What if a mortgage application needs the same credit score check? Or a car loan needs the same income check? You copy the code or create awkward shared utility methods.
4. Inflexible Configuration Want to skip the debt check for premium customers? Or make the loan amount limit configurable per branch? You add more if statements inside an already tangled method.
5. No Clear Rejection Reason When a loan is rejected it is hard to trace exactly which rule caused it especially as the number of checks grows.
What We Really Need

["Break each check into its own isolated handler.","Let each handler decide approve and pass it on, or reject and stop.","Allow new checks to be added, removed, or reordered without touching existing code.","Keep each check clean, focused, and independently testable."]
items: Break each check into its own isolated handler.
Let each handler decide approve and pass it on, or reject and stop.
Allow new checks to be added, removed, or reordered without touching existing code.
Keep each check clean, focused, and independently testable.

blocks.content: This is exactly what the Chain of Responsibility Pattern provides.
2. Understanding Chain of Responsibility Pattern
The Chain of Responsibility Pattern allows a request to be passed along a chain of handlers. Each handler can either:
["Handle the request and stop the chain","Pass it to the next handler","Handle the request and then pass it along"]
items: Handle the request and then pass it along

blocks.content: This decouples the sender from the receivers giving you the flexibility to compose chains dynamically, reuse logic, and avoid rigid conditional blocks.

Real-World Analogy

Think about a loan application at a bank.

You submit your application at the front desk. The clerk does a basic document check. If documents are fine, it moves to the credit department. The credit officer checks your score. If that passes, it goes to the income verification team. If that clears, a senior manager does the final approval.

You the applicant just submit at the start. The application flows through the chain until someone approves or rejects it. You never deal with each department individually.

The Chain of Responsibility Pattern works exactly the same way the client sends a request to the first handler, and it flows through the chain until one handler stops it or it reaches the end.
blocks.title: Note

blocks.content: Class Diagram
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1778245814277-a614e4de.png
The Three Participants

Handler Interface LoanHandler Declares the common interface for all handlers. Defines setNext() to link handlers together and handle() to process a request. Every handler in the chain is treated uniformly the client never knows which concrete handler it is talking to.

Abstract Base Handler BaseLoanHandler Holds the reference to the next handler and provides the forward() method that concrete handlers call to pass the request along. This avoids repeating the chaining logic in every concrete handler.

Concrete Handlers CreditScoreHandler, IncomeHandler, DebtCheckHandler, LoanAmountHandler Each implements one check. Decides whether to reject the application and stop the chain, or call forward() to pass it to the next handler. Each handler is completely independent and knows nothing about the others.
Client Builds the chain by linking handlers with setNext() and sends the application to the first handler. Completely unaware of which handler ultimately approves or rejects it.
3. How It Works
The Chain of Responsibility workflow follows a clear delegation sequence:
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1778245814646-cfda02a2.png
Step 1 The client creates concrete handler objects CreditScoreHandler, IncomeHandler, DebtCheckHandler, LoanAmountHandler.
Step 2 The client links them using setNext(), forming the chain in the desired order.
Step 3 The client sends the loan application to the first handler CreditScoreHandler.
Step 4 Each handler runs its check. If the application passes, it calls forward() to push it to the next handler. If it fails, the handler rejects it and the chain stops immediately.
Step 5 This continues until a handler rejects the application or it clears all checks and gets approved at the end.
4. Implementing Chain of Responsibility
Let's refactor our monolithic LoanProcessor into a clean, extensible chain of modular handlers.

blocks.content: Notice how clean this is. No conditional logic orchestrating the steps. Each handler is isolated and focused on one rule. Adding a new check likeEmploymentVerificationHandlerorAgeCheckHandleronly requires creating a new class and plugging it into the chain zero changes to existing handlers.
What We Achieved
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1778245815546-3c6e5aca.jpg
5. Practical Example: Employee Leave Approval

A second example to reinforce the pattern. An employee submits a leave request. The request passes through a chain of approvers each one can approve it directly if it falls within their authority, or pass it up the hierarchy.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1778245815803-d53a1980.png
The key difference from the loan example here the chain does not reject, it escalates. Each handler either approves or passes upward. This is the "escalate until handled" variant of the pattern.
Output

--- Alice requests 2 days ---
TeamLead: Approved 2 days for Alice

--- Bob requests 7 days ---
TeamLead: 7 days exceeds limit. Escalating to Manager...
Manager: Approved 7 days for Bob

--- Carol requests 20 days ---
TeamLead: 20 days exceeds limit. Escalating to Manager...
Manager: 20 days exceeds limit. Escalating to Director...
Director: Approved 20 days for Carol

--- Dave requests 45 days ---
TeamLead: 45 days exceeds limit. Escalating to Manager...
Manager: 45 days exceeds limit. Escalating to Director...
Director: 45 days exceeds authority. Escalating to HR...
No approver available. Request pending HR review.
